transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-05-07
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20290507-7634 (link)

Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (Northwind VP Eng), Sofia Alvarez (Head of Cloud), Tom Becker (Security Architect), Lena Cho (Platform Eng)

Auto-summary (auto): Customer needs private inference with strict region gating, BYOK/HSM, static egress for firewall allowlisting.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thank you for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, that's Ethan who is our solutions engineer. 
[00:05] Rajiv: Hey, thanks for the time. We, uh, wanted to, kind of, walk through our constraints and see the best path forward between Dedicated vs Private.
[00:12] Maya: Totally. Quick ask — can folks mute if not speaking? Cool. Sofia, do you want to kick us off with the topology?
[00:19] Sofia: Sure. So, high level we're multi-cloud but primarily on AWS. We also have an On‑Prem Outposts environment in EMEA for low-latency inference near our EU customers. Our requirement is that data and inference traffic must stay in EU or US regions only — so no APAC routing, no cross-region egress.
[00:35] Ethan: Got it. When you say stay in EU or US, is that policy at the account level or per-model? Like do some models run in different places?
[00:42] Sofia: Account level for the first phase. We'll want geo-fencing at the networking layer; routing must never egress to other cloud regions.
[00:49] Tom: And from security we need static egress IPs for allowlisting by our customers, plus support for BYOK where keys are in our HSM cluster — FIPS 140-2 compliant.
[00:58] Maya: Okay, yeah those are good constraints. We do private deployments with customer VPCs; options are Private with PrivateLink/private endpoints and Transit Gateway for scale, or Dedicated where we reserve capacity and peer into your VPCs.
[01:10] Rajiv: What's the tradeoff for peering vs PrivateLink? Latency and operational complexity mostly.
[01:15] Ethan: Peering/Transit gives you normal VPC-to-VPC routing which is simpler for high-throughput, but you need to manage route tables and TGW attachments. PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink/private endpoints) isolates the service side and can be easier from security policies — you get ENIs in your account and your egress stays local. PrivateLink also avoids transitive issues with TGW but can be slightly higher on per-connection setup overhead.
[01:33] Sofia: And IDs, IP ranges — we'd prefer less config if it's less brittle.
[01:36] Ethan: Right. Also for static egress IPs we typically put a NAT/proxy in the customer VPC or we can allocate a set of egress IPs from our side if using Dedicated — depends on how the routing is configured.
[01:47] Tom: When you say allocate egress IPs from your side, does that mean Redwood would own those IPs and we'd have to allowlist them?
[01:53] Maya: Yes, in Dedicated mode we can announce a set of egress IPs per customer for outbound calls so the customer only needs to allowlist those. For PrivateLink the egress path would typically remain inside your VPC and egress through your NATs — so you'd control the external IPs.
[02:05] Rajiv: How about latency: our target is p50 80ms for short text generation calls for internal services. Is that achievable with PrivateLink?
[02:13] Ethan: 80ms p50 is achievable if the model is colocated in the same region and if we use warm caches. The key is keeping KV cache locality and minimizing cross-AZ hops. PrivateLink will not add meaningful latency — the bigger factor is whether the inference runtime is colocated and whether we need to fetch large context from your systems.
[02:29] Lena: We do have some datasets that live in our Outposts and we want inference to happen near them to avoid hauling data to a central region.
[02:36] Ethan: For Outposts we can run Redwood Private within your Outposts VPC — it's basically an on‑prem extension of AWS VPC. We'll need to validate kernel/AMI compatibility with the runtime but it's supported in previous engagements.
[02:47] Tom: BYOK — how does Redwood integrate with customer KMS/HSM? We can't have keys exported.
[02:52] Maya: We support Bring Your Own Key patterns. For Private we can integrate with your KMS via IAM roles and endpoint policies; for the HSM you keep the keys and we call KMS using a cross-account role; Redwood never stores plaintext keys. Ethan, want to add?
[03:03] Ethan: Yeah, we have a plugin model for KMS integration. For customers needing HSM, we do an attested TLS session and we can use a KMIP bridge where necessary. The important part is we don't import keys into our control plane for BYOK flows.
[03:15] Tom: KMIP bridge — is that documented? We need to show our auditors.
[03:18] Maya: We'll include our security pack and the HSM/KMS integration doc in the follow up.
[03:21] Rajiv: Are there any required route table changes that might break existing VPC patterns? We have strict subnet segmentation.
[03:27] Ethan: Minimal if using PrivateLink. You'll create interface endpoints (ENIs) in the subnets you choose. For Transit Gateway or peering, you'd need new route table entries and attachments which could impact segmentation if not planned.
[03:39] Sofia: We also use strict egress controls — no internet egress allowed from some subnets. How do we allow the model to pull occasional updates?
[03:46] Maya: You could route update fetches through a controlled subnet with NAT gateway and egress allowlist, or we can push model artifacts to an S3 bucket in your account using a pre-signed transfer, so no outbound is necessary. That is often preferred for locked-down environments.
[03:58] Rajiv: On the topic of model artifacts, any caveats for quantized models / kernel compatibility on Outposts?
[04:02] Ethan: We test the runtime on customer compute. Small differences in CPU instruction sets can matter for quantization runtimes; we'll do a quick compatibility test during the pilot to validate inference kernels. For GPUs on Outposts we need the right drivers and NVidia runtime versions.
[04:16] Tom: Audit logging — we need request-level logs for all inference calls for a 180-day retention and the logs must include request IDs, model versions, and whether the cache was hit.
[04:25] Maya: Redwood Console provides per-route logs and token-level cost breakdowns. For Private we can forward logs to your SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch or an S3 sink — we'll include the retention policy.
[04:36] Ethan: Note that high-volume logging will affect cost; we can sample or push structured summaries and still capture full traces on alert.
[04:43] Sofia: For geo-locking, do you have region blacklisting at the control plane? We don't want admin mistakes to accidentally spin up a model in Singapore.
[04:51] Maya: Yes, customers can pin allowed regions at the org level; the control plane will prevent creating private endpoints or deploying to disallowed regions. We'll enforce that via policy and we'll reflect it in RBAC.
[05:00] Rajiv: Great. Timeline — we want a working pilot in 3 weeks. Is that realistic?
[05:04] Ethan: It's tight but doable if we get your VPC layout and NAT/eips, and if you can onboard a sandbox Outposts test node. A typical pilot is 2–4 weeks depending on approvals.
[05:12] Maya: For pilot success criteria let's define: 1) endpoints reachable over PrivateLink/TGW, 2) p50 latency under 100ms for test prompt set, 3) BYOK integration validated, 4) egress IPs allowlisted and log forwarding established.
[05:25] Tom: That seems fair. Also, we need to validate disaster recovery: if a region goes down can traffic failover to another allowed region? But only within EU/US boundaries.
[05:36] Ethan: Failover is supported — you can configure automated fallback policies. We can restrict the fallback to allowed regions only. There is a tradeoff: failover might increase latency temporarily as caches are cold.
[05:48] Rajiv: Pricing — if we go Dedicated and Redwood announces egress IPs, is the pricing materially different vs PrivateLink?
[05:54] Maya: Dedicated involves reserved capacity so it will have a committed monthly fee plus usage; PrivateLink in a hosted model is pay-as-you-go. We'll share a TCO comparison.
[06:03] Lena: Operationally, we want to avoid many route table changes. PrivateLink with ENIs looks easier for us. Is there any limit to the number of ENIs or endpoints?
[06:11] Ethan: AWS has limits per account, but you can request increases. For scale we often combine PrivateLink with TGW patterns for multi-VPC architectures.
[06:20] Sofia: Question — can Redwood pull logs directly into our SIEM via encrypted transfer?
[06:24] Maya: Yes, CloudWatch/Kinesis/S3 integrations available; we'll provide the architecture examples.
[06:29] Tom: A quick note from compliance — our auditors want explicit statements about where keys are used and whether Redwood staff can access them.
[06:35] Maya: We'll provide the BYOK attestation and a statement that Redwood personnel cannot access customer keys for BYOK flows; access to logs and telemetry can be restricted.
[06:41] Rajiv: Any gotchas for cross-account roles and PrivateLink? We have separate accounts for prod and sandbox.
[06:46] Ethan: We'll need cross-account IAM roles and endpoint policies; it's standard but requires careful mapping of principals. We'll include a template.
[06:53] Sofia: Ok, so next steps: send security pack, sample network diagram, and schedule a follow-up workshop.
[06:58] Maya: Yep. We'll also ask for your current NAT/egress IP ranges and the subnet list.
[07:02] Rajiv: We'll compile that and send. Thanks.
[07:05] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the workshop and the docs.
